newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus Airways sees 7mln pound loss in 97.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus Airways sees 7mln pound loss in 97.

text.p: Cyprus's national carrier Cyprus Airways is looking at a seven million pound loss in 1997 and possible bankruptcy by 1999 if nothing is done to reverse its dire finances, its chairman said on Monday.

The ominous warning came from the newly appointed chairman of the majority state-owned carrier, Takis Kyriakides, speaking at a parliamentary committee on the future of the debt-ridden airline and ways to pull it out of the red and into the black.
"Cyprus Airways can quickly go bankrupt," Kyriakides told MPs. "There has been a prediction capital and reserves will be drained by the end of 1999 unless new capital is invested."
Of the loss forecast this year, Cyprus Airways will post a loss between five and six million, and charter subsidiary Eurocypria between 1 and 1.5 million, Kyriakides said.
The company reported a preliminary consolidated pre-tax loss of 2.15 million pounds in 1996, compared to a pre-tax profit of 5.03 million in 1995.
Cyprus Airways is 80 percent owned by the government, and its remainder is traded on the Cyprus Stock Exchange.
Under bourse regulations, the government must reduce its holding stake in the company to less than 70 percent within the next 24 months through the floatation of new shares.
But looking at the current state of the company, such a possibility is unlikely, Kyriakides said.

"A new issue of shares is unrealistic taking into account today's situation in the airline. We need a credible plan to reverse the trend. Only then will be able to talk about raising capital from private investors," said Kyriakides.
The company has commissioned British consultants Arthur DeLittle to come up with a new strategic plan, which will be completed within three months.
The company has blamed falling load factors, its comparatively high number of staff and low productivity in an environment becoming rapidly competitive as the key reasons for the decline.
Kyriakides said that dropping loss-making routes, cutting down on overtime work and enacting an early retirement scheme may be in the pipeline. Only 13 of 42 routes are profitable.
The government, he added, has been asked to stay the total deregulation of flights from the holiday island for two years at least.

Kyriakides said the company was looking at the possibility of renewing its fleet structure by disposing a number of planes with a large number of seats and replacing them with 80 and 100 seat aircraft.
They could be used on short-distance flights and to launch a shuttle service between Cyprus and Athens, its most profitable route, he said.
